Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Immigration and asylum Hundreds of asylum seekers removed from UK to France have disappeared, say NGOs Rights groups say those missing after being deported under one in, one out deal include dozens of age-disputed children UK politics live – latest updates Diane Taylor Fri 11 Sep 2026 07.33 EDT Last modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 09.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hundreds of asylum seekers including at least 41 age-disputed children who were removed to France under the “one in, one out” deal have disappeared, human rights organisations have said. The pilot scheme was hailed as “groundbreaking” by the former prime minister Keir Starmer when he and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, announced it in July 2025. Under a treaty drawn up for this agreement, it forcibly returns small-boat asylum seekers to France in exchange for others brought legally to the UK from France. ‘I would rather die than return to France’: the brutal reality of the UK’s one in, one out scheme Read more The deal is due to expire on 1 October and at the moment it is not known what, if anything, will replace it. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, is reportedly pushing for the deal to be extended and scaled up, and the French government has indicated it wants the scheme to be expanded Europe-wide rather than France having to accept small-boat returnees alone. One French politician told the Guardian that so far France’s overtures to other countries to take back a share of small-boat asylum seekers had received a negative response. View image in fullscreen A refugee folding a blanket at a makeshift camp on the outskirts of Calais. Photograph: Kiran Ridley/Getty Images About 1,400 small-boat arrivals have been returned to France since September 2025, just 4% of 32,000 who have crossed the Channel since the deal was signed. These figures do not include the significant minority who have come back to the UK a second time, some of whom are now living under the radar here. The UK and France amended the treaty to allow for people returning to the UK in lorries to be sent back to France a second time. At a meeting in parliament this week chaired by Mike German, a general rapporteur on asylum and migration policy for the parliamentary assembly of the Council of Europe, and Alex Sobel, the new chair of parliament’s joint committee on human rights, parliamentarians were told about the disappearances and other concerns about the scheme by NGO representatives working on the ground. Maddie Harris, the director of the Humans For Rights Network, said several NGOs had between them compiled a list of at least 41 age-disputed children and young people whom they claimed had been unlawfully returned to France. It is unlawful to detain lone children in adult immigration detention centres, and they are excluded from the one in, one out treaty. The Home Office disputed this and told the Guardian: “This is categorically untrue. Nobody has been returned to France where their age is in dispute. “Every detained person is advised of their right to legal representation and how they can obtain such representation within 24 hours of arrival at an immigration removal centre. Age assessments are carried out to maintain the integrity of our border, while ensuring those genuinely under 18 receive the appropriate support.” View image in fullscreen A screengrab from video issued by the Home Office shows Border Force officers processing small-boat migrants, including biometric and security checks, before their relocation to an immigration removal centre to await their return to France. Photograph: Home Office/PA However, the prisons and detention Independent Monitoring Boards have reported that almost a hundred children had been identified as unlawfully detained as adults for the scheme. The IMBs’ interim chair, Jane Leech, attended the meeting and raised concerns that some people were being unlawfully detained for the scheme because the Home Office was “detaining more people than they can remove”. French politicians have told the Guardian that only 200 people forcibly returned to France were still in contact with the authorities there, with hundreds of others having gone underground in countries across Europe. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion The Guardian has interviewed dozens of returnees who are no longer in contact with the French authorities and are living underground in Europe. They say they have disappeared due to hostility from the French authorities, pressure to return to their home countries where they believe they will be unsafe, or the threat of being forced back to other European countries such as Bulgaria that they passed through on their journeys. Home Office sources said that what happened to people once they were returned to France was a matter for the French authorities. France’s interior ministry declined to comment on the disappearances. View image in fullscreen Border Force officers processing small-boat arrivals detained under the one in, one out deal at the Manston immigration centre in Kent. Photograph: Home Office/PA Harris said the forced return of lone children to France was “shameful”. She said: “We support many children detained under this scheme and attempt to secure their release. However, at least 41 children have been removed from the UK to France and their whereabouts is currently unknown. The vast majority of these children have experienced acute violence and exploitation and are now without protection somewhere in Europe.” Nihal Osman, a programme coordinator for Médecins Sans Frontières, told the parliamentary meeting that asylum seekers were returned to France from the UK in a “deeply concerning” condition, with many displaying severe psychological symptoms such as flashbacks, acute anxiety, self-harm, suicidal thoughts and psychological breakdown. “What we are witnessing is the accumulation of trauma on trauma,” she said. Sobel said he was “deeply concerned” about the ongoing securitisation of the French border to prevent asylum seekers crossing the Channel to the UK. “The French police are doing things it would be unacceptable for British police to do,” he said. Photograph: Ben Booth/Sopa Images/Shutterstock Nottingham Woman arrested over shooting of police officer in Nottingham Aisha Zaman, 27, charged with two firearms offences after incident in city centre on Sunday Guardian staff Thu 22 Oct 2026 15.52 EDT Last modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 15.59 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 27-year-old woman has been charged over the shooting of a police officer in Nottingham . Aisha Zaman, from the Hyson Green area of the city, has been charged with possession of a prohibited firearm and possession of that firearm with intent to commit an indictable offence. A weapon was recovered and a large crime scene cordon put in place around Angel Row in the heart of the city after the incident at 4.50am on Sunday. Nottinghamshire police said the officer was approaching two suspects when he was hit by a bullet. He remains in hospital receiving treatment.
